claim: Human code reading is mixed, goal-driven switching between top-down hypotheses and bottom-up chunking, not one fixed strategy; as-needed reading of only the relevant code is the common pattern in large programs.
agent_test: Compare a fixed linear-read prompt against a goal-first, read-only-what-is-relevant prompt on repo QA tasks at equal tokens.

claim: Experts do not read code linearly; they skip toward execution order, but experience effects on linearity replicate only partly (vertical moves yes, NW score no).
agent_test: Test whether reading in call/execution order beats file order in the agent's context at equal tokens.

claim: Ko and Uttl: three strategy clusters in an unfamiliar language; breadth-first (2.00 bugs) and spec-focused (1.65) fixed more bugs than depth-first info-seeking (1.00), N=75, one study, one task, an unfamiliar language.
agent_test: Run breadth-first (survey all modules then dive) versus depth-first (dive on first hit) exploration on bug finding at equal tokens.

claim: Pennington: control-flow (program model) forms before function (situation model). An OO replication found situation-model questions answered better than program-model ones, so the order depends on paradigm and study phase.
agent_test: Ask control-flow questions before function-level questions versus the reverse and measure downstream modification correctness.

claim: Gilmore: comprehension happens inside the debugging loop and is triggered by expectation-code mismatch, not as a finished model built first.
agent_test: Compare read-all-then-debug against hypothesise-run-observe loops on bug fixing at equal tokens.

claim: A hypothesis-experiment-observation loop around a debugger helps LLM repair only modestly (Defects4J v1.2: 87 vs 76 fixes; v2.0: 110 vs 113 for the baseline), and hallucinated debugger output lowers plausible-patch odds by about 11 points.
agent_test: Replicate with real tool output only, never model-simulated execution, at equal tokens.

claim: LLMs lean on identifier names (beacons): removing names drops class-summary accuracy by 11 to 29 points and execution prediction by 10 to 14 points; fault localisation breaks under meaning-preserving edits (78% of correct localisations fail).
agent_test: Run the agent with intact and scrambled names on a code-understanding set; add a rule to verify claims from structure, not names.

claim: LLM mental simulation of execution is unreliable: average 44.4% accuracy, IC 10.3 over 15 models; of coherent simulations only 46.92% give the right output; best model fully traced 47% of tasks.
agent_test: Compare a model-simulated trace with real tool execution on the same bugs at equal tokens.

claim: A fixed top-down localisation pipeline (file, then skeleton, then lines) matches open-ended agents on SWE-bench Lite at low cost: 32.00% at $0.70; skeleton view 58.33% vs full file 53.67% and cheaper.
agent_test: Skeleton-first versus full-file reading in the agent at equal tokens.

claim: How code is shown to an agent changes success: a 100-line viewer scores 18.0% vs 12.7% for full file and 14.3% for 30 lines; one failed edit cuts eventual success from 90.5% to 57.2%.
agent_test: Vary window size of code views at equal tokens on a bug-fix set.

claim: Agent failure is mostly fine-grained localisation and long trajectories, not file finding: file-level match 92-97% for successes vs 59-81% for failures; agent line recall 0.15-0.23 against oracle 0.95.
schema_part: S1/S2 (stop and re-plan on long reading)
agent_test: Add a reading step budget and a forced hypothesis restatement; compare trajectory length and success.

claim: Human-model attention alignment on code is weak: at most 22% of methods show significant human-model rank correlation, next-line follow-up accuracy is 47% vs 42.3% baseline, and alignment does not predict summary quality.
agent_test: Not a scaffold lever; caution against claiming the agent reads like a human.

claim: Human structural complexity metrics (McCabe, Cognitive Complexity, size) predict human understandability weakly and predict LLM success poorly (AUROC 0.63 vs 0.86 for a shadow model).
agent_test: Check whether metric-based triage of functions beats uniform reading in the agent.

claim: Programmers judging LLM-written assertions accept correct ones 73.9% but reject incorrect ones only 49.0% (chance) at equal confidence; with a docstring 62% of responses were top-down, so comments anchor judgement. Boundary: in LLMs the anchoring is strong for output prediction (CodeCrash) but not for security-vulnerability review (Thornton).
agent_test: Have the agent review code with and without an adjacent comment and see whether wrong-but-commented code is accepted more.

claim: AI explanations anchored to code can help comprehension (90.2% vs 65.0% in one study) but LLM explanations are often partly wrong (50% had an incorrect statement in Balse et al.).
agent_test: Compare agent summaries with and without line anchors and an explicit check pass.

claim: Code-comprehension experiments are methodologically thin: 95 experiments, median 34 participants, 53.7% students only, only 6 of 25 between-subject designs balanced skill, one qualifying replication.
agent_test: Caution when weighing human findings in the schema.

claim: Fluid intelligence, visual perception and speed predict comprehension correctness (standardised beta 0.299, 0.261, 0.247) while crystallised intelligence and personality do not.
agent_test: No direct test; weak hint that reasoning capacity, not stored knowledge, drives reading success.

claim: Atoms of confusion raise error rates in C (professionals) and Java (novices; pooled OR 3.82, 7 of 14 atoms significant), and LLM perplexity spikes align with human EEG (rho 0.37) on them.
agent_test: Prompt the agent to list confusing micro-patterns before tracing and compare error rate.

claim: Snippet-level LLM perplexity does not reliably track human understandability (largest correlation 0.373, not significant) although token-level spikes track local confusion.
agent_test: Test perplexity as a trigger for re-reading at token level versus snippet level.

claim: Reasoning-tuned LLMs find the same obfuscation levels hard as humans; instruction- and coder-tuned models show near-zero alignment.
agent_test: Check whether adding a reasoning step before reading raises human-like difficulty alignment.

claim: A model fine-tuned on psychology data (Centaur) predicts human program-comprehension answers modestly better than its base (NLL 1.63 vs 1.85, effect 0.172, better in 7 of 9 studies).
agent_test: Not a scaffold lever.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: No published study found implements von Mayrhauser-Vans or Letovsky as an explicit agent prompt and tests it against a control; the mapping from these models to agent design is untested.
agent_test: Build the three-way test: bottom-up, top-down and as-needed prompts at equal tokens.

claim: Bottom-up comprehension of obfuscated code activates working-memory-related left-hemisphere regions (17 participants, FDR p<0.01), supporting a load story for bottom-up reading.
agent_test: No direct test.

claim: Chain-of-thought reasoning about code stage by stage (trace paths, simulate patches, audit against the issue, predict test inputs/outputs) raises issue resolution by 6 to 10 points on SWE-bench Pro at about 8% more tokens; gain is not yet reproduced by others.
agent_test: Add a stage-wise trace-and-simulate step to the read states and compare at equal tokens against plain read-then-fix.

claim: A fill-in reasoning certificate (premises, execution traces, conclusion) beats free chain of thought without running code: patch equivalence 78.2% to 88.8%, code QA +9 to +11 points, at about 2.8x the steps.
agent_test: Test a certificate template for 'does this code do X' questions with and without a step cap.

claim: Structured mental simulation can beat real reproduction-test execution on localisation (method recall 0.66 vs 0.23 for a 28-test executor), so execution is not automatically better than careful reading; no clean ablation exists.
agent_test: Run simulate-only, run-only, and simulate-then-run arms on the same localisation set.

claim: LLMs treat code comments as authoritative on output prediction: misleading comments or prints cost about 24% relative accuracy, chain of thought halves the loss (23.2% to 13.8%); but security-review detection is not shifted by adversarial comments (p>0.21).
agent_test: Add a rule: derive behaviour from code first, check comments as claims; test with wrong comments planted.

claim: Hiding identifier names costs little on short code (CRUXEval relative drop about 1-9%) and more on longer code (LiveCodeBench up to 27%); no two-pass 'structure first, names second' test exists.
agent_test: Test a first pass with names masked, then a second pass with names, on name-misleading code.

claim: Structure added as a hint or an extra view helps repo agents modestly (call/inheritance comments Func@5 +2.2, variance halved; graph views +20 to +46 resolved of 731), while a graph-only tool lost to grep (Func@5 0.595 vs 0.832).
agent_test: Give a skeleton plus who-calls-me links as hints; keep text search available.

claim: Preview-first, load-on-demand reading (as-needed) cuts localisation tokens about 10-15% with equal or slightly better accuracy; depth-first traversal is bundled with other changes so breadth vs depth is untested for agents.
agent_test: Compare preview-first vs full-file reading at equal accuracy target and count tokens.

claim: One re-plan at the first source edit (median at 60% of the trajectory) beats rule-based stuck detection and nearly matches periodic review at 11-15% of its planner cost.
agent_test: Insert one plan-check before the first edit; compare with step-count triggers.

claim: Von Mayrhauser and Vans name three reasons a hypothesis fails (no verifying code found; one code satisfies several hypotheses; code cannot be explained) and say to keep open hypotheses manageable; Letovsky questions are why, how, and data-description.
agent_test: Make these operators: state hypothesis, seek beacon, label failure reason, cap open hypotheses.

claim: LLM perplexity spikes on small code regions track human EEG confusion (rho 0.47 on confusing snippets, 0.05 on clean; 24 participants), while whole-snippet perplexity does not predict human difficulty well.
agent_test: Use token-level surprise as a 're-read here' flag and measure false positives on clean code.
